newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Britain asks EU to tackle computer "millenium bug".
newsitem.headline: Britain asks EU to tackle computer "millenium bug".

text.p: British Science and Technology Minister Ian Taylor tried again on Thursday to get his European Union partners to pay more attention to a computer programming problem that could wreak havoc at the turn of the century.

Dubbed the "millenium bug", the threat results from the fact that computer systems use a two-digit format to show the year -- making 1997, for example, simply 97. At the turn of the century, many will interpret 00 as 1900 rather than 2000.
Taylor told a meeting of EU telecommunications ministers that European companies were still not aware enough of the problem -- the third time he has raised the issue with them.

"If a substantial number of companies in Europe fail to modify their computer systems to deal with the Century Date Change, we could rapidly see a breakdown in many of the normal communications between companies," he said in a letter to EU Telecoms Commissioner Martin Bangemann before the meeting.
He urged the EU to follow the lead of Britain, which has undertaken a publicity campaign to educate industry -- including sending letters to 120,000 company chief executives last week.

Bangemann told reporters the EU was funding research into software that could address the problem and that an EU working group of Commission, business, science and government experts had been in touch with industry groups about it.

He said some sectors, for example banking and insurance, were more concerned than others. "Despite the sexiness of the subject it seems to be rather difficult to get the public in any way exercised about this," he said.
He told Reuters the Commission would help raise awareness, but "the bulk has to be done by industry itself".
